title: Every answer is a statistic
summary: One measurement is one coin flip. Estimating anything takes many — and precision is expensive.

shots.title:
One shot
isn't an answer.
shots.subtitle: Quantum computers return **samples**. Turning samples into numbers has a cost.
shots.narration: Here is something the hype usually skips. A quantum computer doesn't hand you a number. It hands you samples.

shots.text: Run a circuit, measure, get one bitstring. Run it **again** — maybe a different one. Each run is called a **shot**.
shots.narration: You run a circuit and measure: you get one bitstring. Run it again and you might get a different one. Each run is called a shot.
Say the true chance of reading one is a quarter. After one shot we know almost nothing. After ten, a rough guess. After a thousand, the frequencies settle close to three quarters and a quarter.

notes: $N$ shots buys an error that shrinks like $1/\sqrt{N}$.
Ten times more precise means a **hundred** times more shots.
shots.narration: The typical error of that estimate shrinks with the square root of the number of shots. Ten times more precision costs a hundred times more shots.
On a log scale it's a straight line, falling one decade for every two decades of samples. Ten thousand shots gets you to about plus or minus zero point four percent here.

shots.text: Banks already live with this law. **Monte Carlo** pricing simulates thousands of random market paths and averages them — error ∝ 1/√N.
shots.narration: Why should a trader care? Because banks already live with this exact law. Monte Carlo pricing simulates random market paths and averages them, and its error shrinks the same way.

shots.text: Unit 4's big idea: **amplitude estimation** beats the square-root law — error ∝ 1/N. Hold that thought.
shots.narration: The headline quantum algorithm for finance, amplitude estimation, is a way to beat the square-root law, with error shrinking like one over N. Hold that thought.

steps.title: Measure, measure, measure
steps.brief: Tilt the qubit to set its odds, then measure in batches. Watch the estimate wander, then settle inside the shrinking band.

questions.prompt: P(1) = 0.25 and you take 10,000 shots. What is the typical error of your estimate, √(p(1−p)/N)? Give a decimal.
You want your estimate to be 10× more precise. How many more shots do you need?
questions.explain: Error ∝ 1/√N, so cutting error by 10 needs N to grow by 10² = 100.

questions.prompt: Which classical finance technique follows the same square-root law?
options: Reading a price off a screen
questions.explain: Monte Carlo averages random samples, so its error shrinks like 1/√N — the target of quantum amplitude estimation.
